title: AI Implementation Guide: From Use-Case Selection to Safe Rollout
description: A practical AI rollout plan covering use-case selection, evaluation datasets, privacy, human review, cost controls, monitoring, and measurable acceptance criteria.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Select a Narrow, Measurable Use Case
sections.body: Start with a repeatable task where the current process is visible and a mistake can be detected before it causes harm. Examples include drafting an internal summary, classifying support requests for human review, or searching approved documentation. Avoid beginning with a vague goal such as 'use AI everywhere.' Record current time per task, volume, error rate, review effort, and who owns the final output. Exclude use cases that require consequential decisions without suitable oversight, evidence, and an approved risk process.

sections.title: Define an Evaluation Set Before Choosing a Vendor
sections.body: Create a representative set of real or safely anonymized examples covering routine cases, edge cases, ambiguous inputs, and known failure modes. Write down what a correct or acceptable answer means for each example before comparing tools. Score factual accuracy, completeness, citation quality where relevant, tone, refusal behavior, latency, and reviewer correction time. Include examples where the system should say it does not know. Re-run the same set after changing the model, prompt, retrieval source, or configuration so improvements and regressions are visible.

sections.title: Compare the Whole Workflow, Not Just the Model
sections.body: An implementation includes more than the model name: input collection, instructions, retrieval, access control, review interface, logging, fallback behavior, and integration with existing systems. During a pilot, test how users correct an answer, report a failure, and continue when the service is unavailable. Compare hosted products, APIs, and self-managed options using the same task set. Record which capabilities are confirmed in current vendor documentation, which are tested internally, and which remain unverified; a polished demo is not enough evidence.

sections.title: Protect Data and Limit Access
sections.body: Classify the data the workflow may receive and decide what must never be sent to the service. Review retention, training-use terms, regional processing, subprocessors, deletion options, and administrative access against your requirements. Use least-privilege permissions, keep secrets out of prompts, and avoid logging sensitive input unless there is a documented need and suitable controls. If retrieval is used, ensure users cannot retrieve documents they are not authorized to access. Confirm reviewers understand how to handle sensitive or unexpected output.

sections.title: Keep Human Review Proportional to Risk
sections.body: Set review rules based on the consequence of an error. Low-risk drafting may need sampling and user correction; customer-facing, financial, legal, security, or safety-related outputs may require mandatory approval or may be unsuitable for automation. Define escalation triggers, known limitations, prohibited outputs, and a safe fallback. Make clear when content is AI-assisted and who owns the final decision. Human review is meaningful only when the reviewer has enough context, time, and authority to reject the output.

sections.title: Budget for Usage and Operational Work
sections.body: Estimate cost from expected volume, input and output size, retries, retrieval, storage, monitoring, and human review—not only the advertised per-request rate. Set per-user or per-workflow limits, alerts, and a kill switch for unexpected usage. Track latency and correction time alongside model charges; a cheaper response can cost more overall if it creates extra review work. Agree on a fallback for rate limits, provider outages, and model changes, and test it before expanding the pilot.

sections.title: Pilot, Monitor, and Decide Whether to Expand
sections.body: Run the pilot with a defined group, start and end date, owner, and written pass/fail criteria. Compare results with the baseline using the same evaluation set and report successful and failed cases. Monitor quality drift, user corrections, cost, latency, security incidents, and changes to vendor terms. Expand only if the workflow meets acceptance criteria and the team can support it. If it fails, narrow the use case, improve source data or review, or stop the deployment; adoption alone is not evidence of value.
